scene.label: Act 1, Scene 4
scene.title: SCENE IV. A room in Doctor Caius's house
scene.location: A room in Doctor Caius's house

lines.text: What, John Rugby!
lines.plainText: What John Rugby

lines.text: I'll go watch.
lines.plainText: I'll go watch

lines.text: Go; and we'll have a posset for't soon at night, in faith, at the latter end of a sea-coal fire.
lines.plainText: Go and we'll have a posset for't soon at night in faith at the latter end of a seacoal fire

lines.text: Ay, for fault of a better.
lines.plainText: Ay for fault of a better

lines.text: And Master Slender's your master?
lines.plainText: And Master Slender's your master

lines.text: Ay, forsooth.
lines.plainText: Ay forsooth

lines.text: Does he not wear a great round beard, like a glover's paring-knife?
lines.plainText: Does he not wear a great round beard like a glover's paringknife

lines.text: No, forsooth, he hath but a little wee face, with a little yellow beard, a Cain-coloured beard.
lines.plainText: No forsooth he hath but a little wee face with a little yellow beard a Caincoloured beard

lines.text: A softly-sprighted man, is he not?
lines.plainText: A softlysprighted man is he not

lines.text: Ay, forsooth. But he is as tall a man of his hands as any is between this and his head. He hath fought with a warrener.
lines.plainText: Ay forsooth But he is as tall a man of his hands as any is between this and his head He hath fought with a warrener

lines.text: How say you? O, I should remember him. Does he not hold up his head, as it were, and strut in his gait?
lines.plainText: How say you O I should remember him Does he not hold up his head as it were and strut in his gait

lines.text: Yes, indeed, does he.
lines.plainText: Yes indeed does he

lines.text: Well, heaven send Anne Page no worse fortune! Tell Master Parson Evans I will do what I can for your master. Anne is a good girl, and I wish—
lines.plainText: Well heaven send Anne Page no worse fortune Tell Master Parson Evans I will do what I can for your master Anne is a good girl and I wish

lines.text: Out, alas! Here comes my master.
lines.plainText: Out alas Here comes my master

lines.text: We shall all be shent. Run in here, good young man, go into this closet. He will not stay long.
lines.plainText: We shall all be shent Run in here good young man go into this closet He will not stay long

lines.text: Vat is you sing? I do not like dese toys. Pray you, go and vetch me in my closet une boîtine verte, a box, a green-a box. Do intend vat I speak? A green-a box.
lines.plainText: Vat is you sing I do not like dese toys Pray you go and vetch me in my closet une botine verte a box a greena box Do intend vat I speak A greena box

lines.text: Ay, forsooth, I'll fetch it you.
lines.plainText: Ay forsooth I'll fetch it you

lines.text: [Aside.] I am glad he went not in himself. If he had found the young man, he would have been horn-mad.
lines.plainText: Aside I am glad he went not in himself If he had found the young man he would have been hornmad

lines.text: Fe, fe, fe fe! Ma foi, il fait fort chaud. Je m'en vais à la cour—la grande affaire.
lines.plainText: Fe fe fe fe Ma foi il fait fort chaud Je m'en vais la courla grande affaire

lines.text: Is it this, sir?
lines.plainText: Is it this sir

lines.text: Oui, mette-le au mon pocket. Dépêche, quickly—Vere is dat knave Rugby?
lines.plainText: Oui mettele au mon pocket Dpche quicklyVere is dat knave Rugby

lines.text: What, John Rugby, John!
lines.plainText: What John Rugby John

lines.text: Here, sir.
lines.plainText: Here sir

lines.text: You are John Rugby, and you are Jack Rugby. Come, take-a your rapier, and come after my heel to the court.
lines.plainText: You are John Rugby and you are Jack Rugby Come takea your rapier and come after my heel to the court

lines.text: 'Tis ready, sir, here in the porch.
lines.plainText: 'Tis ready sir here in the porch

lines.text: By my trot, I tarry too long. 'Od's me! Qu'ay j'oublié? Dere is some simples in my closet dat I vill not for the varld I shall leave behind.
lines.plainText: By my trot I tarry too long 'Od's me Qu'ay j'oubli Dere is some simples in my closet dat I vill not for the varld I shall leave behind

lines.text: Ay me, he'll find the young man there, and be mad!
lines.plainText: Ay me he'll find the young man there and be mad

lines.text: O diable, diable! Vat is in my closet? Villainy! Larron! [Pulling Simple out.] Rugby, my rapier!
lines.plainText: O diable diable Vat is in my closet Villainy Larron Pulling Simple out Rugby my rapier

lines.text: Good master, be content.
lines.plainText: Good master be content

lines.text: Wherefore shall I be content-a?
lines.plainText: Wherefore shall I be contenta

lines.text: The young man is an honest man.
lines.plainText: The young man is an honest man

lines.text: What shall de honest man do in my closet? Dere is no honest man dat shall come in my closet.
lines.plainText: What shall de honest man do in my closet Dere is no honest man dat shall come in my closet

lines.text: I beseech you, be not so phlegmatic. Hear the truth of it. He came of an errand to me from Parson Hugh.
lines.plainText: I beseech you be not so phlegmatic Hear the truth of it He came of an errand to me from Parson Hugh

lines.text: Vell?
lines.plainText: Vell

lines.text: Ay, forsooth, to desire her to—
lines.plainText: Ay forsooth to desire her to

lines.text: Peace, I pray you.
lines.plainText: Peace I pray you

lines.text: Peace-a your tongue!—Speak-a your tale.
lines.plainText: Peacea your tongueSpeaka your tale

lines.text: To desire this honest gentlewoman, your maid, to speak a good word to Mistress Anne Page for my master in the way of marriage.
lines.plainText: To desire this honest gentlewoman your maid to speak a good word to Mistress Anne Page for my master in the way of marriage

lines.text: This is all, indeed, la! But I'll ne'er put my finger in the fire, and need not.
lines.plainText: This is all indeed la But I'll ne'er put my finger in the fire and need not

lines.text: Sir Hugh send-a you?—Rugby, baille me some paper.—Tarry you a little-a while.
lines.plainText: Sir Hugh senda youRugby baille me some paperTarry you a littlea while

lines.text: [Aside to Simple.] I am glad he is so quiet. If he had been throughly moved, you should have heard him so loud and so melancholy. But notwithstanding, man, I'll do you your master what good I can; and the very yea and the no is, the French doctor, my master—I may call him my master, look you, for I keep his house, and I wash, wring, brew, bake, scour, dress meat and drink, make the beds, and do all myself—
lines.plainText: Aside to Simple I am glad he is so quiet If he had been throughly moved you should have heard him so loud and so melancholy But notwithstanding man I'll do you your master what good I can and the very yea and the no is the French doctor my masterI may call him my master look you for I keep his house and I wash wring brew bake scour dress meat and drink make the beds and do all myself

lines.text: [Aside to Mistress Quickly.] 'Tis a great charge to come under one body's hand.
lines.plainText: Aside to Mistress Quickly 'Tis a great charge to come under one body's hand

lines.text: [Aside to Simple.] Are you avised o' that? You shall find it a great charge, and to be up early and down late; but notwithstanding—to tell you in your ear, I would have no words of it—my master himself is in love with Mistress Anne Page; but notwithstanding that, I know Anne's mind. That's neither here nor there.
lines.plainText: Aside to Simple Are you avised o' that You shall find it a great charge and to be up early and down late but notwithstandingto tell you in your ear I would have no words of itmy master himself is in love with Mistress Anne Page but notwithstanding that I know Anne's mind That's neither here nor there

lines.text: You jack'nape, give-a dis letter to Sir Hugh. By gar, it is a shallenge. I will cut his troat in de park, and I will teach a scurvy jackanape priest to meddle or make. You may be gone, it is not good you tarry here.—By gar, I will cut all his two stones. By gar, he shall not have a stone to throw at his dog.
lines.plainText: You jack'nape givea dis letter to Sir Hugh By gar it is a shallenge I will cut his troat in de park and I will teach a scurvy jackanape priest to meddle or make You may be gone it is not good you tarry hereBy gar I will cut all his two stones By gar he shall not have a stone to throw at his dog

lines.text: Alas, he speaks but for his friend.
lines.plainText: Alas he speaks but for his friend

lines.text: It is no matter-a ver dat. Do not you tell-a me dat I shall have Anne Page for myself? By gar, I vill kill de Jack priest; and I have appointed mine host of de Jarteer to measure our weapon. By gar, I will myself have Anne Page.
lines.plainText: It is no mattera ver dat Do not you tella me dat I shall have Anne Page for myself By gar I vill kill de Jack priest and I have appointed mine host of de Jarteer to measure our weapon By gar I will myself have Anne Page

lines.text: Sir, the maid loves you, and all shall be well. We must give folks leave to prate. What, the good-year!
lines.plainText: Sir the maid loves you and all shall be well We must give folks leave to prate What the goodyear

lines.text: Rugby, come to the court with me. [To Mistress Quickly.] By gar, if I have not Anne Page, I shall turn your head out of my door.—Follow my heels, Rugby.
lines.plainText: Rugby come to the court with me To Mistress Quickly By gar if I have not Anne Page I shall turn your head out of my doorFollow my heels Rugby

lines.text: You shall have An—fool's head of your own. No, I know Anne's mind for that. Never a woman in Windsor knows more of Anne's mind than I do, nor can do more than I do with her, I thank heaven.
lines.plainText: You shall have Anfool's head of your own No I know Anne's mind for that Never a woman in Windsor knows more of Anne's mind than I do nor can do more than I do with her I thank heaven

lines.text: [Within.] Who's within there, ho?
lines.plainText: Within Who's within there ho

lines.text: Who's there, I trow? Come near the house, I pray you.
lines.plainText: Who's there I trow Come near the house I pray you

lines.text: How now, good woman? How dost thou?
lines.plainText: How now good woman How dost thou

lines.text: The better, that it pleases your good worship to ask.
lines.plainText: The better that it pleases your good worship to ask

lines.text: What news? How does pretty Mistress Anne?
lines.plainText: What news How does pretty Mistress Anne

lines.text: In truth, sir, and she is pretty, and honest, and gentle; and one that is your friend, I can tell you that by the way, I praise heaven for it.
lines.plainText: In truth sir and she is pretty and honest and gentle and one that is your friend I can tell you that by the way I praise heaven for it

lines.text: Shall I do any good, think'st thou? Shall I not lose my suit?
lines.plainText: Shall I do any good think'st thou Shall I not lose my suit

lines.text: Troth, sir, all is in His hands above. But notwithstanding, Master Fenton, I'll be sworn on a book she loves you. Have not your worship a wart above your eye?
lines.plainText: Troth sir all is in His hands above But notwithstanding Master Fenton I'll be sworn on a book she loves you Have not your worship a wart above your eye

lines.text: Yes, marry, have I; what of that?
lines.plainText: Yes marry have I what of that

lines.text: Well, thereby hangs a tale. Good faith, it is such another Nan! But, I detest, an honest maid as ever broke bread. We had an hour's talk of that wart. I shall never laugh but in that maid's company. But, indeed, she is given too much to allicholy and musing. But for you—well, go to.
lines.plainText: Well thereby hangs a tale Good faith it is such another Nan But I detest an honest maid as ever broke bread We had an hour's talk of that wart I shall never laugh but in that maid's company But indeed she is given too much to allicholy and musing But for youwell go to

lines.text: Well, I shall see her today. Hold, there's money for thee. Let me have thy voice in my behalf. If thou seest her before me, commend me.
lines.plainText: Well I shall see her today Hold there's money for thee Let me have thy voice in my behalf If thou seest her before me commend me

lines.text: Will I? I' faith, that we will! And I will tell your worship more of the wart the next time we have confidence, and of other wooers.
lines.plainText: Will I I' faith that we will And I will tell your worship more of the wart the next time we have confidence and of other wooers

lines.text: Well, farewell, I am in great haste now.
lines.plainText: Well farewell I am in great haste now

lines.text: Farewell to your worship.
lines.plainText: Farewell to your worship
